problem: The torque conclusion is wrong and contradicts the book's own formula T = bmep × V_d / (2π n_R). With n_R = 2 in the denominator, the four-stroke gives HALF the torque of the two-stroke, not twice. As written the answer also contradicts itself: if the four-stroke had twice the torque at the same speed it would also make twice the power, not half.
fix: T = bmep × V_d / (2π n_R), so at the same bmep, swept volume and speed the two-stroke (n_R = 1) makes twice the torque of the four-stroke (n_R = 2), because it completes one cycle every revolution instead of every second revolution. BP = bmep × V_d × N / n_R, so the two-stroke also makes twice the power at the same speed.

problem: The answer says bmep 'stays nearly constant over the useful speed range', but bmep is proportional to torque at fixed swept volume, so it rises to a peak and falls exactly as the torque curve does (Section 4 of this chapter says so). The real reason bmep is fairer is that it normalises by swept volume, not that it is flat with speed.
fix: Torque and bmep rise and fall together with speed, so flatness is not the point. Torque of a big engine is large simply because its swept volume is large. bmep divides the work per cycle by V_d, so engines of 100 cc and 10 L are reduced to the same scale and their breathing and combustion quality can be compared directly.
